sections.name: Linux Mastery & Hardening
sections.explanation_simple: Linux is the operating system that powers most of the internet (servers, cloud, supercomputers, Android, and most hacking tools). Learning Linux security is essential because: 1) Most servers run Linux, so understanding it helps you secure them, 2) All security distributions like Kali Linux and Parrot OS are Linux-based, 3) Linux gives you total control over everything. Security in Linux is about permissions (who can read/write/execute what), monitoring (who's doing what), and hardening (turning off unnecessary services to reduce attack surface). Think of Linux like a building with many rooms - permissions are the keys that open specific doors, and hardening is locking rooms you don't need so nobody can sneak in.
key_concepts: Root vs User: Root is all-powerful admin, regular users have limited permissions
SUID/GUID: Special permissions that let a program run as its owner (security risk if misused)
SELinux/AppArmor: Mandatory Access Control - even root can't bypass these rules
Chroot/Jail: Isolating a process to a specific directory (can't see the rest of the system)
Namespaces: Linux feature that isolates processes (foundation of Docker containers)
Cgroups: Control groups limit how much CPU/memory a process can use
Capabilities: Instead of full root, give specific privileges (CAP_NET_RAW for ping)
PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules): Pluggable authentication system (password, biometric, 2FA)
Auditd: Linux audit system - logs every system call for forensics
Systemd-journald: Logging system (view with journalctl)
AppArmor/SELinux Profiles: Define exactly what a program can access (files, network, capabilities)
Kernel Modules: Loadable drivers that run in kernel space (malicious ones = rootkits)

code_examples.title: Linux Server Hardening Script
code_examples.code:
#!/bin/bash
# ===== LINUX SERVER HARDENING SCRIPT =====
# Run as root on a fresh Ubuntu/Debian server

set -e  # Exit on any error

echo "=== LINUX HARDENING STARTED ==="

# 1. UPDATE SYSTEM
apt update && apt upgrade -y
apt autoremove -y

# 2. CREATE ADMIN USER (instead of using root)
ADMIN_USER="sysadmin"
useradd -m -G sudo $ADMIN_USER
passwd $ADMIN_USER

# 3. HARDEN SSH
cat >> /etc/ssh/sshd_config << 'EOF'
Port 2222                              # Change default port (22 -> 2222)
PermitRootLogin no                     # No direct root login
PasswordAuthentication no              # SSH keys only
PubkeyAuthentication yes
MaxAuthTries 3                         # 3 attempts then disconnect
ClientAliveInterval 300                # Disconnect idle sessions after 5 min
ClientAliveCountMax 0
AllowUsers sysadmin                    # Only this user can SSH
Protocol 2
EOF

systemctl restart sshd

# 4. SET UP FIREWALL (UFW)
ufw default deny incoming
ufw default allow outgoing
ufw allow 2222/tcp comment "SSH"
ufw allow 80/tcp comment "HTTP"
ufw allow 443/tcp comment "HTTPS"
ufw --force enable

# 5. FAIL2BAN (Brute force protection)
apt install fail2ban -y
cat > /etc/fail2ban/jail.local << 'EOF'
[DEFAULT]
bantime = 3600
findtime = 600
maxretry = 5

[sshd]
enabled = true
port = 2222
logpath = %(sshd_log)s
EOF
systemctl enable fail2ban
systemctl start fail2ban

# 6. AUTO UPDATES
apt install unattended-upgrades -y
dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades

# 7. DISABLE UNUSED SERVICES
systemctl disable avahi-daemon 2>/dev/null || true
systemctl disable cups 2>/dev/null || true
systemctl disable bluetooth 2>/dev/null || true

# 8. SECURE SHARED MEMORY
chmod 1777 /dev/shm  # Restrict shared memory

# 9. KERNEL HARDENING
cat >> /etc/sysctl.conf << 'EOF'
# IP Spoofing protection
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1
net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 1

# Ignore ICMP redirects
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0

# Disable source packet routing
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0

# SYN flood protection
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1
net.ipv4.tcp_syn_retries = 2

# Log martian packets
net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians = 1
EOF

sysctl -p

echo "=== LINUX HARDENING COMPLETE ==="
echo "Important: Now add your SSH public key to ~$ADMIN_USER/.ssh/authorized_keys"
echo "Then test SSH on port 2222 before closing this session!"

code_examples.title: Linux Forensics: Investigating a Compromised System
code_examples.code:
#!/bin/bash
# ===== INCIDENT RESPONSE: LINUX FORENSICS =====
# Run these commands to investigate a potentially compromised system

echo "=== COLLECTING FORENSIC DATA ==="

# 1. RUNNING PROCESSES
ps auxf > /tmp/forensics/processes.txt
# Look for: strange names, base64 encoded commands, high CPU

# 2. NETWORK CONNECTIONS
netstat -tulpn > /tmp/forensics/network.txt
ss -tulpn >> /tmp/forensics/network.txt
# Look for: unknown services listening, connections to strange IPs

# 3. CHECK FOR ROOTKITS
# Common rootkit detection:
lsmod | grep -E "(hide|hook|sysfs)"  # Suspicious kernel modules
cat /proc/modules | grep -E "[hidden]"  # If you see 'hidden', something is hiding

# 4. CHECK SCHEDULED TASKS (cron)
cat /etc/crontab
ls -la /etc/cron.*/
for user in $(cut -f1 -d: /etc/passwd); do
    crontab -u $user -l 2>/dev/null
done
# Look for: scripts in /tmp, downloads from strange URLs

# 5. CHECK STARTUP SCRIPTS
ls -la /etc/init.d/
ls -la /etc/systemd/system/
ls -la ~/.bashrc  # User-level persistence
ls -la ~/.ssh/authorized_keys  # Unauthorized SSH keys

# 6. CHECK RECENT FILES
find / -mmin -60 -type f 2>/dev/null | head -50  # Files modified in last hour

# 7. LOG ANALYSIS
tail -100 /var/log/auth.log     # Authentication attempts
tail -100 /var/log/syslog       # System events
journalctl -u ssh --since "24 hours ago"  # SSH logs
journalctl -u fail2ban          # Brute force attempts

# 8. CHECK BINARY INTEGRITY
debsums -e 2>/dev/null | grep -v "OK$"  # Check if any system files were modified
# Or rpm -Va for RedHat-based

# 9. EXAMINE ACTIVE CONNECTIONS
lsof -i
# Check for reverse shells: /dev/tcp, /dev/udp connections

# 10. MEMORY FORENSICS (requires root)
# dd if=/dev/mem of=/tmp/forensics/memory.dump bs=1M
# Then analyze with volatility: volatility -f memory.dump imageinfo

sections.name: Windows Internals & Security
sections.explanation_simple: Windows security is a constant battle between usability and protection. Windows is the most attacked OS because it has the largest user base. Understanding Windows internals - how the kernel, registry, services, and authentication work - is essential for both securing Windows systems and understanding how attacks work. Key areas: Active Directory (the central authentication system for corporate networks), Group Policy (centralized security settings), PowerShell (powerful but dangerous if hijacked), and the Windows event logging system (your eyes into what's happening on the system).
key_concepts: Active Directory (AD): Microsoft's directory service - manages users, computers, permissions across network
Domain Controller: Server that runs AD (the 'king' of the Windows network)
Group Policy: Centralized configuration management (password policies, software restrictions, etc.)
LSASS: Local Security Authority Subsystem Service - handles authentication (prime target for credential theft)
NTLM: Older Windows authentication protocol (vulnerable to relay attacks)
Kerberos: Modern Windows authentication (ticket-based, more secure than NTLM)
SAM: Security Account Manager - stores local user password hashes
NTDS.dit: Active Directory database file (contains ALL domain password hashes - THE target)
Windows Defender: Built-in antivirus/EDR (pretty good now, bypass is an art)
Event Viewer/Event Logs: Windows logging system (Security, Application, System logs)
PowerShell Logging: Script block logging, module logging, transcript logging (attackers try to bypass these)
UAC (User Account Control): Prompts when programs need admin access (bypass techniques exist)
Registry: Windows configuration database (persistence, settings, malware loves it)
Windows Services: Background processes (attackers install malicious services)
Token: Windows' version of a permission set (determines what a process can do)
Scheduled Tasks: Windows task scheduler (another common persistence method)

code_examples.title: Windows Security Audit PowerShell Script
code_examples.code:
# ===== WINDOWS SECURITY AUDIT (PowerShell) =====
# Run as Administrator

Write-Host "=== WINDOWS SECURITY AUDIT ===" -ForegroundColor Cyan

# 1. CHECK LOCAL ADMINISTRATORS
Write-Host "`n[!] Local Administrators:" -ForegroundColor Yellow
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" | Format-Table Name, ObjectClass, PrincipalSource

# 2. CHECK FOR STALE USER ACCOUNTS
Write-Host "`n[!] Disabled/Inactive Users:" -ForegroundColor Yellow
Search-ADAccount -UsersOnly -AccountDisabled | Select-Object Name, SamAccountName
Search-ADAccount -UsersOnly -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90 | Select-Object Name, SamAccountName

# 3. AUDIT SERVICES
Write-Host "`n[!] Non-Microsoft Services Running:" -ForegroundColor Yellow
Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq "Running" -and $_.DisplayName -notlike "*Microsoft*" -and $_.DisplayName -notlike "*Windows*")}

# 4. CHECK OPEN PORTS
Write-Host "`n[!] Listening Ports:" -ForegroundColor Yellow
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object LocalPort, OwningProcess | Sort-Object LocalPort

# 5. CHECK SCHEDULED TASKS
Write-Host "`n[!] Suspicious Scheduled Tasks:" -ForegroundColor Yellow
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object {$_.TaskPath -notlike "*Microsoft*" -and $_.State -eq "Ready"} |
    Select-Object TaskName, TaskPath, State

# 6. EXAMINE POWERSHELL LOGGING
Write-Host "`n[!] PowerShell Logging Status:" -ForegroundColor Yellow
$scriptLogging = Get-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging" -Name "EnableScriptBlockLogging" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
$transcription = Get-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription" -Name "EnableTranscripting" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Write-Host "Script Block Logging: $(if ($scriptLogging.EnableScriptBlockLogging -eq 1) { 'Enabled' } else { 'DISABLED!' })"
Write-Host "Transcription: $(if ($transcription.EnableTranscripting -eq 1) { 'Enabled' } else { 'DISABLED!' })"

# 7. CHECK WINDOWS DEFENDER STATUS
Write-Host "`n[!] Windows Defender Status:" -ForegroundColor Yellow
Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AntivirusEnabled, RealTimeProtectionEnabled, LastQuickScanTime, LastFullScanTime

# 8. EVENT LOG ANALYSIS (Failed logins)
Write-Host "`n[!] Failed Login Attempts (last 24h):" -ForegroundColor Yellow
$failedLogins = Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; ID=4625} -MaxEvents 50 |
    Select-Object TimeCreated, @{N='User';E={$_.Properties[5].Value}}, @{N='SourceIP';E={$_.Properties[18].Value}}
$failedLogins | Format-Table TimeCreated, User, SourceIP -AutoSize

# 9. CHECK FOR UNUSUAL STARTUP PROGRAMS
Write-Host "`n[!] Startup Programs:" -ForegroundColor Yellow
Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Select-Object Name, Command, Location

# 10. AUDIT REGISTRY AUTORUNS
Write-Host "`n[!] Registry Autoruns:" -ForegroundColor Yellow
$autorunPaths = @(
    "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run",
    "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce",
    "HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run",
    "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
)
foreach ($path in $autorunPaths) {
    if (Test-Path $path) {
        Get-ItemProperty -Path $path | Select-Object -ExpandProperty PSObject.Properties |
            Where-Object {$_.MemberType -eq 'NoteProperty'} |
            Select-Object @{N='Location';E={$path}}, Name, Value
    }
}

code_examples.title: Active Directory Attack & Defense
code_examples.code:
# ===== ACTIVE DIRECTORY SECURITY =====
# Understanding common attacks and their mitigations

"""
COMMON AD ATTACK VECTORS:

1. KERBEROASTING
   Attack: Request TGS tickets for service accounts, crack offline
   Defense: Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA), long complex passwords for SPNs

2. AS-REP ROASTING
   Attack: Find accounts without Kerberos pre-authentication, crack AS-REP response
   Defense: Ensure all users have "Do not require Kerberos preauthentication" DISABLED

3. PASS-THE-HASH (PtH)
   Attack: Use NTLM hash directly instead of password (no cracking needed!)
   Defense: Enable Credential Guard, use LSA protection, don't use NTLM if possible

4. PASS-THE-TICKET (PtT)
   Attack: Steal Kerberos TGT/TGS tickets and use them to authenticate
   Defense: Limit ticket lifetime, monitor for anomalous Kerberos usage

5. GOLDEN TICKET
   Attack: Forge a Kerberos TGT using KRBTGT hash (if you get this, you OWN the domain)
   Defense: Protect KRBTGT hash at all costs, rotate KRBTGT password regularly

6. SILVER TICKET
   Attack: Forge a service ticket (TGS) to access a specific service
   Defense: Use extended protection for authentication, monitor Kerberos events

7. DCSYNC
   Attack: Replicate AD database using Directory Replication Service (get ALL hashes)
   Defense: Limit who can replicate AD, monitor for replication events (Event ID 4662)

8. LLMNR/NBT-NS POISONING
   Attack: Respond to name resolution broadcasts, capture NTLM hashes
   Defense: Disable LLMNR and NetBIOS via Group Policy
"""

# PowerShell: Check for common AD misconfigurations
function Test-ADSecurity {
    Write-Host "=== ACTIVE DIRECTORY SECURITY CHECK ===" -ForegroundColor Cyan

    # Check for Kerberos pre-auth disabled
    Get-ADUser -Filter {DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true} -Properties DoesNotRequirePreAuth |
        Select-Object Name, SamAccountName |
        ForEach-Object { Write-Host "[!] AS-REP Roastable: $($_.Name)" -ForegroundColor Red }

    # Check for service accounts with weak passwords
    Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -like '*'} -Properties ServicePrincipalName, PasswordLastSet |
        Select-Object Name, ServicePrincipalName, PasswordLastSet |
        ForEach-Object { Write-Host "[i] Service Account: $($_.Name) - SPN: $($_.ServicePrincipalName)" }

    # Check delegation settings
    Get-ADUser -Filter {TrustedForDelegation -eq $true} -Properties TrustedForDelegation, ServicePrincipalName |
        Select-Object Name |
        ForEach-Object { Write-Host "[!] Unconstrained Delegation: $($_.Name)" -ForegroundColor Red }

    # Check for privileged groups
    $groups = @('Domain Admins', 'Enterprise Admins', 'Schema Admins', 'Backup Operators', 'Server Operators')
    foreach ($group in $groups) {
        $members = Get-ADGroupMember -Identity $group | Select-Object Name
        if ($members) {
            Write-Host "`n[$group Members]:" -ForegroundColor Yellow
            $members | ForEach-Object { Write-Host "  - $($_.Name)" }
        }
    }
}

sections.name: Mobile Security: Android & iOS
sections.explanation_simple: Mobile security is about protecting the billion+ phones and tablets in use. Android is more open (you can install apps from anywhere, sideload APKs, root the device) which means more flexibility but also more attack surface. iOS is locked down (only Apple's App Store, no file system access without jailbreaking) which is more secure by default but creates a 'walled garden'. Mobile app testing involves decompiling the app (turning the .apk/.ipa back into code), analyzing how it communicates with servers, checking for insecure data storage, and testing for vulnerabilities like other platforms.
key_concepts: APK (Android Package): The Android app file format (basically a zip with compiled code + resources)
IPA (iOS App Store Package): The iOS app file format (encrypted by Apple)
JADX: Tool that decompiles APK to readable Java code
Smali: Assembly language for Android's Dalvik VM (what you see when you decompile at lowest level)
Frida: Dynamic instrumentation tool - inject JavaScript into running apps to modify behavior
Objection: Runtime mobile exploration powered by Frida
MobSF: Mobile Security Framework - automated security analysis for Android and iOS
Root Detection: Apps checking if device is rooted (attackers bypass this)
SSL Pinning: App only accepts a specific certificate (prevents MITM - attackers bypass this)
Keychain (iOS): Secure storage for passwords, keys on iOS
Keystore (Android): Same for Android (hardware-backed on modern devices)
Jailbreak Detection: iOS equivalent of root detection
App Sandboxing: iOS and Android isolate apps from each other
Runtime Hooking: Modifying app behavior while it's running (Frida's specialty)
DexGuard/ProGuard: Android code obfuscation (makes reverse engineering harder)
